Adult male Mayan cichlids exhibit a maximum total length of 39.4 centimeters [Li = 39.4 centimeters], a size that makes them one of the largest cichlids native to the Neotropical region. This ultimate length is achieved only after several years of sustained growth, during which individuals transition through distinct ontogenetic niches. Females typically remain somewhat smaller, although the species as a whole displays modest sexual size dimorphism. The robust body shape and large adult size are adaptations that facilitate territorial defense and the excavation of nesting sites in the soft substrates of coastal lagoons and slow-moving freshwater rivers. This species, Mayaheros urophthalmus, is also notable for its broad salinity tolerance, which allows it to occupy habitats ranging from nearly fresh inland waters to hypersaline mangrove creeks. Within these environments, large males frequently monopolize access to spawning sites, and their ultimate body length plays a significant role in determining social dominance and reproductive success. The growth trajectory of males is characterized by a rapid juvenile phase followed by a prolonged period of asymptotic growth in the later adult stage, a pattern typical of many large-bodied Neotropical cichlids.

Sexual maturation in the Mayan cichlid is first attained at a total length of 11.7 centimeters [Lp = 11.7 centimeters], a body size that corresponds roughly to the end of the first year of life under optimal thermal conditions. At this length, individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic resources to support the energetic demands of gonadal development and the initiation of reproductive behavior. The associated wet weight at puberty has been documented at 45.5 grams [Wwp = 45.5 grams], a mass that reflects a substantial investment in both structural tissue and energy reserves. This threshold size for maturation is relatively small compared to the maximum body size of the species, suggesting a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive opportunity against continued somatic growth. In the fluctuating environments of the Yucatán Peninsula, early maturation may confer a selective advantage by allowing individuals to reproduce before the onset of unfavorable dry-season conditions. The attainment of sexual maturity at this length also coincides with the development of the characteristic coloration and fin morphology used in agonistic displays and courtship rituals.

The reproductive output of the Mayan cichlid is remarkably high, driven by the production of multiple clutches during each extended breeding season. At a stable water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], a single gravid female can produce as many as 6615 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 6615 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity that places this species among the most prolific of its lineage. This large clutch size is complemented by a high frequency of spawning, as females can repeat the event up to 360 times per year [F_R_i = up to 360 times per year] under the same thermal regime. Such an extraordinary reproductive rate reflects the species' adaptation to unpredictable hydrologic conditions, where a single successful spawning season can contribute disproportionately to population recruitment. The combined annual fecundity, resulting from both large clutch sizes and frequent spawning, ensures that the species can rapidly colonize newly inundated habitats following seasonal rains. Field observations in the Celestún Biosphere Reserve have confirmed that breeding activity peaks during the summer months, when water temperatures are consistently elevated.

Newly hatched larvae of the Mayan cichlid emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small wet weight of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available for endotrophic development. This tiny neonatal size places the species at the lower end of the cichlid spectrum and necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding after chorion rupture. The yolk-sac larvae are initially lecithotrophic for a brief period, typically two to three days, before the mouth opens and first prey capture begins. The small birth mass is a direct consequence of the modest egg diameter, which in this species is comparable to that reported for Oreochromis niloticus, a related tilapiine cichlid. Despite this seemingly vulnerable start, the high fecundity and intensive biparental nest guarding counterbalance the risks associated with a small larval body size. Larvae that successfully complete the exotrophic transition then enter a period of rapid mass gain, with growth rates strongly modulated by prevailing water temperature and the abundance of microcrustacean prey.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult males has been estimated at 1840 grams [Wwi = 1840 grams], a substantial body mass that when combined with a maximum lifespan of approximately 3285 days [am = approximately 3285 days] under the warm conditions typical of the species' native range at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], underscores the capacity for prolonged somatic investment after maturation. This combination of large adult mass and extended longevity is characteristic of a relatively slow life-history pace among Neotropical cichlids, particularly when compared to small-bodied congeners that complete their life cycle in under two years. The long lifespan allows individuals to experience multiple breeding seasons and to accumulate the social experience necessary to secure and defend high-quality territories. Senescence in this species is gradual, with a decline in reproductive output and somatic condition becoming apparent only in the oldest individuals, typically those exceeding five years of age. The interplay between adult body mass, longevity, and reproductive output defines the species' demographic resilience in the face of environmental stochasticity.
